source: In GB-A1, GB-A2, and GB-S4, which contained two or more distant metastatic lesions, the clonal composition of tissues obtained from the same or adjacent organs showed a similar tendency, while the clonal composition of anatomically distant organs was distinct from each other.
evidence: Supported by comparative clonal composition analysis of metastatic sites.

claim: In GB-A1, abdominal wall 1–4 did not contain clone C.
source: In GB-A1 (Figure 2A), abdominal wall 1–4 did not contain clone C, and liver 1–3 did not contain clone F.
evidence: Supported by clonal composition analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In GB-A1, liver 1–3 did not contain clone F.
source: In GB-A1 (Figure 2A), abdominal wall 1–4 did not contain clone C, and liver 1–3 did not contain clone F.
evidence: Supported by clonal composition analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In GB-A1, omentum 1–2 had a high prevalence of clone F of over 27.0%.
source: In addition, omentum 1–2 had a high prevalence of clone F of over 27.0%.
evidence: Supported by clonal prevalence analysis of omentum metastases.

claim: In GB-A2, clone G was more prevalent in lung and chest wall lesions than clone F.
source: In GB-A2 (Figure 3A), as opposed to clone G, which was more prevalent in lung and chest wall lesions, clone F was more prevalent in liver and mesentery lesions.
evidence: Supported by clonal prevalence comparison shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In GB-A2, clone F was more prevalent in liver and mesentery lesions than clone G.
source: In GB-A2 (Figure 3A), as opposed to clone G, which was more prevalent in lung and chest wall lesions, clone F was more prevalent in liver and mesentery lesions.
evidence: Supported by clonal prevalence comparison shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In GB-A2, chest wall and mesentery metastases developed later than lung and liver metastases.
source: In clinical information of the GB-A2 patient, chest wall and mesentery metastases developed later than lung and liver metastases.
evidence: Supported by clinical timeline data.

claim: In GB-S4, proportions of clones G and H were specifically high in distant LN and colon wall metastasis, respectively.
source: In GB-S4 (Figure 3B), proportions of clones G and H were specifically high in distant LN and colon wall metastasis, respectively.
evidence: Supported by clonal prevalence analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Signatures 1, 3, and 13 were commonly dominant in all three datasets (SNUBH, MSKCC, and Shanghai).
source: Signatures 1, 3, and 13 were commonly dominant in all three datasets, while signatures 22 and 24 were exclusive in our dataset (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by comparative mutational signature analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Signatures 22 and 24 were exclusive in the SNUBH dataset.
source: Signatures 1, 3, and 13 were commonly dominant in all three datasets, while signatures 22 and 24 were exclusive in our dataset (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by comparative mutational signature analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The limited number of SNVs and small indels per sample (median 61, range 12–241) made it difficult to compare among individual tumors.
source: In our dataset, the limited number of SNVs and small indels per sample (median 61, range 12–241) made it difficult to compare among individual tumors (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on assessment of data limitations with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: At the metastasis phase, signatures 1 and 13 decreased compared with early and late carcinogenesis.
source: At the metastasis phase, signatures 1 and 13 decreased while signatures 22 and 24 increased compared with early and late carcinogenesis.
evidence: Supported by comparative mutational signature analysis across evolutionary stages.

claim: At the metastasis phase, signatures 22 and 24 increased compared with early and late carcinogenesis.
source: At the metastasis phase, signatures 1 and 13 decreased while signatures 22 and 24 increased compared with early and late carcinogenesis.
evidence: Supported by comparative mutational signature analysis across evolutionary stages.

claim: Aristolochic acid is an ingredient of oriental herbal medicine.
source: Aristolochic acid is an ingredient of oriental herbal medicine (Debelle et al., 2008; Hoang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on aristolochic acid.

claim: Aflatoxin is known to be contained in soybean paste and soy sauce.
source: In addition, aflatoxin is known to be contained in soybean paste and soy sauce (Ok et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to study on aflatoxin in food products.

claim: Aristolochic acid and aflatoxin might have little impact on the early stage of cancer development, but their impacts might be highlighted in overt cancer cells.
source: Taken together, the two carcinogens might have little impact on the early stage of cancer development, but their impacts might be highlighted in overt cancer cells.
evidence: Based on inference from mutational signature patterns across evolutionary stages.

claim: In GB-A1, ERBB2 copy number gain might have initiated from the precancerous stage and further progressed during the malignant transformation of BilIN.
source: In GB-A1, ERBB2 copy number gain might have initiated from the precancerous stage and further progressed during the malignant transformation of BilIN.
evidence: Based on inference from copy number analysis comparing BilIN and primary tumor.

claim: In GB-A1, ERBB2 copy number was 3 in BilIN and 9 in primary tumors.
source: ERBB2 copy number (Figure 5A and B) was 3 and 9 in concurrent BillN and primary tumors, respectively.
evidence: Supported by copy number analysis shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: In GB-A1, the increased copy number of ERBB2 was maintained after distant metastasis.
source: The increased copy number of ERBB2 was maintained after distant metastasis (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by copy number analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In GB-A1, ERBB2 copy number per cell ranged from 1 to 5 in BilIN by HER2 SISH.
source: HER2 (=ERBB2) silver in situ hybridization (SISH) (Figure 5C and D) was conducted and ERBB2 copy number per cell ranged from 1 to 5 in BilIN, and from 2 to 14 in primary GBAC.
evidence: Supported by SISH analysis shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: In GB-A1, ERBB2 copy number per cell ranged from 2 to 14 in primary GBAC by HER2 SISH.
source: HER2 (=ERBB2) silver in situ hybridization (SISH) (Figure 5C and D) was conducted and ERBB2 copy number per cell ranged from 1 to 5 in BilIN, and from 2 to 14 in primary GBAC.
evidence: Supported by SISH analysis shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: In GB-A1, ERBB2/CEP17 ratio was 2.48 in BilIN and 6.00 in primary GBAC.
source: ERBB2/CEP17 ratio was 2.48 and 6.00 in BilIN and primary GBAC, respectively (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by SISH analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In GB-A1, HER2 IHC results were 2+/3 in the BilIN and 3+/3 in primary GBAC.
source: The HER2 IHC results were 2+/3 in the BillN and 3+/3 in primary GBAC.
evidence: Supported by IHC analysis.

claim: In GB-S6 and GB-S7, ERBB2 amplification was uniformly identified from primary tumors to metastatic tumors.
source: In GB-S6 and GB-S7 (Figure 3D and E), ERBB2 amplification was uniformly identified from primary tumors to metastatic tumors.
evidence: Supported by copy number analysis shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: This is the first study to investigate clonal evolution from precancerous lesions to metastatic tumors in patients with GBAC.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to investigate clonal evolution from precancerous lesions to metastatic tumors in patients with GBAC.
evidence: Based on literature review and novelty claim.

claim: A previous study in colorectal cancer demonstrated a stepwise carcinogenesis model from adenoma to invasive carcinoma by the accumulation of mutations, called the adenoma-carcinoma sequence.
source: A previous study in colorectal cancer by Vogelstein and colleagues demonstrated a stepwise carcinogenesis model from the precancerous lesion, adenoma, to invasive carcinoma by the accumulation of mutations, called the adenoma-carcinoma sequence (Vogelstein et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vogelstein's study.

claim: Recent studies on esophageal squamous cell carcinoma have reported that not only dysplasia but also histologically normal epithelia frequently harbor cancer-driving mutations.
source: In addition, recent studies on esophageal squamous cell carcinoma have reported that not only dysplasia but also histologically normal epithelia frequently harbor cancer-driving mutations (Chen et al., 2017; Yokoyama et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on esophageal cancer.

claim: A recent study on GBAC reported that CTNNB1 mutation was frequently observed (5 out of 11) when BilIN and primary GBAC coexist.
source: A recent study on GBAC (Lin et al., 2021) reported that CTNNB1 mutation was frequently observed (5 out of 11) when BilIN and primary GBAC coexist.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lin et al. study.

claim: In a recent study on GBAC, ERBB2 alteration was found in 36.4% of cases.
source: In addition, ERBB2 alteration was found in 36.4%.
evidence: Inferred to be from the same recent study (Lin et al., 2021) mentioned in the previous sentence.

claim: Two previous studies on GBAC reported the prevalence of ERBB2 alteration as low as 7.9% and 9.4%, respectively.
source: On the other hand, two previous studies on GBAC (Narayan et al., 2019; Li et al., 2014) reported the prevalence of ERBB2 alteration as low as 7.9% and 9.4%, respectively.
evidence: Supported by citations to Narayan and Li studies.

claim: Race or lifestyle differences might have contributed to the difference in ERBB2 alteration prevalence.
source: Race or lifestyle differences might have contributed to the difference.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed differences in ERBB2 prevalence.

claim: Previous studies suggest that subclonal diversity increases through branching evolution during progression and metastasis.
source: Previous studies suggest that subclonal diversity increases through branching evolution during progression and metastasis (Turajlic and Swanton, 2016; Hong et al., 2015; Yachida et al., 2010; Minussi et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on cancer evolution.

claim: It was previously thought that metastasis is initiated by the migration of a single cell to another organ.
source: Previously, it was thought that metastasis is initiated by the migration of a single cell to another organ (Nowell, 1976).
evidence: Supported by citation to historical model of metastasis.

claim: Recent data suggest that polyclonal seeding occurs due to the migration of a cluster of cancer cells.
source: However, recent data suggest that polyclonal seeding occurs due to the migration of a cluster of cancer cells (Turajlic et al., 2019; Cheung and Ewald, 2016; Ullah et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies on polyclonal metastasis.

claim: The study found the possibility of metastasis-to-metastasis spread in GB-A2.
source: Our study found the possibility of metastasis-to-metastasis spread in GB-A2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: Based on inference from phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In recent studies on prostate and breast cancers, metastasis-to-metastasis spread was frequent.
source: In recent studies on prostate and breast cancers, metastasis-to-metastasis spread was frequent (Ullah et al., 2018; Gundem et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on prostate and breast cancer metastasis.

claim: SMAD4 mutations have been associated with distant metastasis and poor prognosis in various cancers, including GBAC.
source: For example, SMAD4 mutations expanded during metastasis in GB-A1 and GB-S3 (Figure 2A and D) and have been associated with distant metastasis and poor prognosis in various cancers, including GBAC (Narayan et al., 2019; Jamal-Hanjani et al., 2017; Yoon et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on SMAD4 in cancer.

claim: The SLIT/ROBO pathway suppresses tumor progression by regulating invasion, migration, and apoptosis.
source: The SLIT/ROBO pathway suppresses tumor progression by regulating invasion, migration, and apoptosis (Gara et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to study on SLIT/ROBO pathway.

claim: The DICER1 gene is associated with pleuropulmonary blastoma in children.
source: The DICER1 gene is associated with pleuropulmonary blastoma in children (Foulkes et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to study on DICER1.

claim: KIAA0100 and CSMD2 are frequently mutated during metastasis in adrenocortical carcinoma.
source: KIAA0100 and CSMD2 are frequently mutated during metastasis in adrenocortical carcinoma (Gara et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to study on adrenocortical carcinoma.

claim: Targeted sequencing data of a single specimen are not enough to determine whether the detected mutations are clonal or subclonal.
source: In this cancer precision medicine era, targeted sequencing data of a single specimen are not enough to determine whether the detected mutations are clonal or subclonal.
evidence: Based on inference from the study's findings about subclonal diversity.

claim: Multi-regional and longitudinal tumor biopsies may not be feasible in most patients unless they underwent surgery and repeated biopsies.
source: However, one caveat is that we cannot easily apply this to real-world patients because multi-regional and longitudinal tumor biopsies may not be feasible in most patients unless they underwent surgery and repeated biopsies.
evidence: Based on practical considerations about clinical feasibility.

claim: Recent studies using circulating tumor DNA have shown the possibility of easily detecting mutations involved in cancer development and progression.
source: Recent studies using circulating tumor DNA have shown the possibility of easily detecting mutations involved in cancer development and progression (Ignatiadis et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to study on circulating tumor DNA.

claim: By detecting clonal mutations from the carcinogenesis stage in healthy individuals, GBAC can be diagnosed at an early stage.
source: By detecting clonal mutations from the carcinogenesis stage in healthy individuals, we can diagnose GBAC at an early stage.
evidence: Speculative application of the study's findings to future clinical practice.

claim: By detecting subclonal mutations in patients with GBAC, expanding subclones can be monitored during follow-up, enabling earlier detection of cancer progression.
source: In addition, by detecting subclonal mutations in patients with GBAC, we can monitor the expanding subclones during follow-up, which enables us to detect cancer progression earlier.
evidence: Speculative application of the study's findings to future clinical practice.

claim: Tumor samples were not acquired according to their developmental sequence due to the impossibility of obtaining samples through frequent biopsies whenever desired.
source: First, it is not possible to obtain samples through frequent biopsies whenever desired. Thus, tumor samples were not acquired according to their developmental sequence.
evidence: Directly stated study limitation.

claim: Due to intratumoral heterogeneity, the clonal composition of a small piece of the tumor may not reflect that of the entire lesion.
source: Second, due to intratumoral heterogeneity, the clonal composition of a small piece of the tumor may not reflect that of the entire lesion (Marusyk et al., 2012).
evidence: Directly stated study limitation with citation.

claim: An accessibility bias was inevitable because the more samples the patient has, the more clones can be identified.
source: Third, as the number of analyzed samples was different among patients, an accessibility bias was inevitable – the more samples the patient has, the more clones we can identify.
evidence: Directly stated study limitation based on sampling methodology.

claim: Patients were eligible for the study if they were diagnosed with GBAC and received surgery between 2013 and 2018 at Seoul National University Bundang Hospital.
source: Patients were eligible for this study if they were diagnosed with GBAC and received surgery between 2013 and 2018 at Seoul National University Bundang Hospital (SNUBH), Seongnam, Korea.
evidence: Directly stated eligibility criteria.

claim: Of the 272 patients who underwent surgery, 9 patients who were able to obtain ≥3 types of tissue and died at the time of analysis were enrolled.
source: Of the 272 patients who underwent surgery, 9 patients who were able to obtain ≥3 types of tissue from among BilIN, GBAC, regional LN metastasis, and distant metastasis and died at the time of analysis were enrolled in the study.
evidence: Directly stated enrollment criteria and numbers.

claim: Two patients who donated their bodies for rapid autopsy were included in the study.
source: In addition, two patients who donated their bodies for rapid autopsy were included in the study.
evidence: Directly stated enrollment information.

claim: The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of SNUBH (IRB No. B-1902/522-303).
source: This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of SNUBH (IRB No. B-1902/522-303).
evidence: Directly stated ethical approval information.

claim: Informed consent was waived because of the retrospective and anonymous nature of the study.
source: Informed consent was waived because of the retrospective and anonymous nature of the study.
evidence: Directly stated ethical consideration.

claim: Library preparation and exome capture was carried out using Agilent SureSelectXT Human All Exon V6.
source: Library preparation and exome capture was carried out using Agilent SureSelectXT Human All Exon V6 (Santa Clara, CA, USA).
evidence: Directly stated methodological detail.

claim: WES was conducted with a paired-end, 100 bp using Illumina NovaSeq 6000.
source: WES was conducted with a paired-end, 100 bp using Illumina NovaSeq 6000 (San Diego, CA, USA).
evidence: Directly stated methodological detail.

claim: The depth of coverage of tumors was at least 300×.
source: The depth of coverage of tumors and normal control samples were at least 300× and 200×, respectively.
evidence: Directly stated sequencing parameter.

claim: The depth of coverage of normal control samples was at least 200×.
source: The depth of coverage of tumors and normal control samples were at least 300× and 200×, respectively.
evidence: Directly stated sequencing parameter.

claim: WES data were analyzed using the Genomon2 pipeline.
source: WES data of GBAC and matched normal samples were analyzed using the Genomon2 pipeline (Institute of Medical Science, University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan; https://genomon.readthedocs.io/ja/latest/, accessed on February 1, 2022).
evidence: Directly stated analytical method.

claim: Sequencing reads were aligned to the human reference genome GRCh37 (hg19) without the 'chr' prefix using Burrows-Wheeler Aligner version 0.7.12.
source: In brief, sequencing reads from adapter-trimmed.fastq files were aligned to the human reference genome GRCh37 (hg19) without the 'chr' prefix using Burrows-Wheeler Aligner version 0.7.12, with default settings.
evidence: Directly stated analytical method.

claim: Gene amplification was defined as a copy number ≥6.
source: Gene amplification was defined as a copy number ≥6 (Wolff et al., 2018).
evidence: Directly stated definition with citation.

claim: Clonal population structure was statistically inferred using PyClone version 0.13.0 with the 'pyclone_beta_binomial' model.
source: These datasets were then used to statistically infer clonal population structure using PyClone version 0.13.0 with the 'pyclone_beta_binomial' model (Roth et al., 2014).
evidence: Directly stated analytical method with citation.

claim: Clonal phylogeny was inferred by CITUP version 0.1.0.
source: Clonal phylogeny was inferred by CITUP version 0.1.0 (Malikic et al., 2015) using cellular prevalence values of each cluster which were generated by PyClone.
evidence: Directly stated analytical method with citation.

claim: CITUP uses information from multiple samples and can infer clonal populations and their frequencies while satisfying phylogenetic constraints.
source: CITUP uses information from multiple samples and can infer clonal populations and their frequencies while satisfying phylogenetic constraints.
evidence: Description of CITUP methodology.

claim: Clusters containing only one mutation were excluded from the input to CITUP if the mutation's role is unclear from previous literature.
source: To ensure accurate tree construction, clusters containing only one mutation were excluded from the input to CITUP if the mutation's role is unclear from previous literature.
evidence: Directly stated methodological decision.

claim: This filter removed 42 mutations from a total of 1577 mutations, representing less than 2.7% of all clustered mutations.
source: This filter removed 42 mutations from a total of 1577 mutations, representing less than 2.7% of all clustered mutations.
evidence: Directly stated impact of filtering.

claim: Analyzed results were visualized using MapScape for multi-regional specimens and TimeScape for longitudinal or putative longitudinal datasets.
source: Analyzed results were visualized using MapScape for multi-regional specimens and TimeScape for longitudinal or putative longitudinal datasets, as appropriate (Smith et al., 2017).
evidence: Directly stated visualization methods with citation.

claim: Mutational signature analysis was conducted using Mutalisk and validated with Signal and MuSiCa.
source: Mutational signature analysis was conducted using Mutalisk (Lee et al., 2018) and validated with Signal (Degasperi et al., 2020) and MuSiCa (Díaz-Gay et al., 2018).
evidence: Directly stated analytical methods with citations.

claim: The COSMIC Mutational Signatures v2 was used as a reference for mutational signature analysis.
source: The COSMIC Mutational Signatures v2 (Alexandrov et al., 2013) was used as a reference.
evidence: Directly stated reference database with citation.

claim: Two public datasets of GBAC from the MSKCC and the Shanghai group were analyzed for comparison.
source: To compare with the other GBAC cohorts, we additionally analyzed two public datasets of GBAC from the MSKCC and the Shanghai group (Narayan et al., 2019; Li et al., 2014), which could be downloaded from the cBioPortal (https://www.cbioportal.org/, accessed on February 1, 2022; Cerami et al., 2012).
evidence: Directly stated comparative analysis with citations.

claim: IHC and SISH analysis of HER2-positive cells was conducted using PATHWAY anti-HER2/neu antibody (4B5; rabbit monoclonal).
source: IHC and SISH analysis of HER2-positive cells was conducted by the board-certified pathologist using PATHWAY anti-HER2/neu antibody (4B5; rabbit monoclonal; Ventana Medical Systems, Tucson, AZ, USA) and a staining device (BenchMark XT, Ventana Medical Systems, Tuscon, AZ, USA), respectively, as previously described (Koh et al., 2019).
evidence: Directly stated methodological detail with citation.

claim: A HER2/CEP17 ratio ≥2.0 was defined as HER2 amplification.
source: Signals from 20 tumor cells were counted and a HER2/CEP17 ratio ≥2.0 was defined as HER2 amplification (Wolff et al., 2018).
evidence: Directly stated definition with citation.

claim: Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used to compare the mean HER2/CEP17 ratio of BilIN versus primary tumor.
source: Wilcoxon rank-sum test is used to compare the mean HER2/CEP17 ratio of BilIN versus primary tumor.
evidence: Directly stated statistical method.
